issues.legal_issue: A lengthy postponement of a mortgagor’s right to redeem is not a clog on the equity of redemption merely because of its duration, where the bargain was fair and was not imposed by taking advantage of the mortgagor’s difficulties.
material_facts: The mortgage deed postponed the right to redeem until eighty-five years after the mortgage was made, and the redemption suit was filed before that period expired.

The mortgage discharged an earlier mortgage and freed other property from that earlier security; the mortgagee accepted a smaller security despite advancing more than the amount secured by the earlier mortgage.
There was no evidence that the mortgagor was financially embarrassed or that the mortgagee took unfair advantage of him; the bargain was found to be fair and made between parties on an equal footing.
issues.conclusion: The eighty-five-year term was enforceable and was not a clog on the equity of redemption. Because the mortgage term had not expired, the redemption suit was premature and was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, the right to redeem arises when the mortgage money becomes due, and ordinarily that is on expiry of the stipulated mortgage term. Although a court may relieve a mortgagor from a bargain restricting redemption, that power is limited by its equitable basis: relief depends on whether the bargain was unconscionable, including whether the lender took advantage of the borrower’s difficult or impecunious position. The length of the term alone does not establish oppression. The Court relied on Vermon v. Bethell and G. and C. Kreglinger v. New Patagonia Meat and Cold Storage Company Ltd. on the basis and limits of equitable intervention, and referred to Santley v. Wilde, Mohammad Sher Khan v. Seth Swami Dayal, and Bakhtawai Begum v. Husaini Khanam on redemption and mortgage terms.

rule.if: mortgage_redemption_suit and redemption_term_not_yet_expired and long_redemption_postponement and no_evidence_of_unfair_pressure and bargain_on_equal_footing

predicates.mortgage_redemption_suit: The proceeding seeks redemption of property given as security for a debt.
predicates.redemption_term_not_yet_expired: The agreed time before the mortgagor may redeem has not ended when the suit is brought.
predicates.long_redemption_postponement: The mortgage agreement postpones redemption for a lengthy period.
predicates.no_evidence_of_unfair_pressure: The evidence does not show that the lender exploited the borrower’s difficulties or financial embarrassment to obtain the term.
predicates.bargain_on_equal_footing: The circumstances show that the parties made the bargain fairly and on an equal footing.

issues.definition: When a redemption suit is brought before a lengthy agreed redemption postponement expires, and the evidence shows neither unfair pressure nor unequal dealing, the suit is premature.

issues.legal_issue: A mortgage term that extinguishes the right to redeem if redemption is not exercised within a limited period, and treats the mortgage as a sale, is invalid, but its invalidity does not invalidate a separate term fixing when the right to redeem first arises.
material_facts: The mortgage deed required the mortgagor to redeem within six months after the eighty-five-year mortgage term expired, failing which the mortgagor would lose all claim to the property and the mortgage deed would be treated as a sale deed.
The term fixing the eighty-five-year period was distinct from the term that purported to extinguish the right to redeem after the six-month window.
The dispute arose in a suit seeking redemption of the mortgage.
issues.conclusion: The term extinguishing the right to redeem after the six-month period was a clog on the equity of redemption and was invalid. The mortgagor’s right to redeem continued after that period, and the invalidity of the forfeiture term did not affect the separate term postponing the right to redeem for eighty-five years.
issues.legal_principle: The rule that a mortgage must remain redeemable, reflected in section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, prevents a contract from taking away the mortgagor’s right to redeem once it has arisen. A term that makes redemption possible only within a specified window and extinguishes the right afterward is invalid; the right continues beyond that window. The invalid term does not invalidate a distinct term fixing when the mortgage money becomes due. The Court relied on Santley v. Wilde for the principle that a mortgage remains redeemable and on Mohammad Sher Khan v. Seth Swami Dayal for the effect of section 60.

rule.if: mortgage_redemption_suit and redemption_limited_to_short_window and failure_to_redeem_extinguishes_right and mortgage_deemed_sale_after_failure

predicates.mortgage_redemption_suit: The proceeding seeks redemption of property given as security for a debt.
predicates.redemption_limited_to_short_window: The mortgage agreement permits redemption only during a specified, limited period after the mortgage becomes redeemable.
predicates.failure_to_redeem_extinguishes_right: The agreement states that the mortgagor loses the right to redeem if that period passes without redemption.
predicates.mortgage_deemed_sale_after_failure: The agreement treats the secured property as sold to the mortgagee if the mortgagor does not redeem within the specified period.

issues.definition: When a mortgage redemption proceeding concerns an agreement that confines redemption to a limited window and extinguishes the right afterward by treating the mortgage as a sale, the forfeiture term is invalid.
